summary: Designs a richer physical and digital student life around the different ways students actually live, study and participate, using evidence-led student personas to shape the experience and hold King’s Edge to account for who can access and benefit from it.
detailSummary:
Student life at King’s is centred on the course, but the wider experience of university also matters: the relationships students build, the communities they join, the opportunities they encounter and the sense that they are genuinely part of King’s.

Students do not experience that wider life in the same way. Their capacity to spend time on campus, participate beyond scheduled study and discover what King’s has to offer is shaped by commuting, paid work, caring responsibilities, disability, placements, patterns of study, confidence, financial pressure and whether they study substantially or entirely online.

This deliverable will use a small set of evidence-led student personas or participation archetypes to represent these different forms of student life. These will provide a practical design and assurance framework for King’s Edge, helping the programme test whether its opportunities, platforms, rhythms and experiences work for students with materially different patterns of time, presence and participation.

Alongside this, King’s will make a deliberate investment in the richness of student life itself. Campuses should become more vibrant, sociable and festival-like environments, filled with visible and low-friction invitations to encounter people, communities, activity and opportunity. Students should have reasons to linger, explore and participate beyond the activity that originally brought them to campus.

Physical presence, however, should not be the price of admission to a rich King’s student life. The same design principles will therefore shape a meaningful digital twin: not simply online replicas of campus activity, but authentic digital routes into community, participation, discovery, shared experiences and opportunity.

Together, this creates a more deliberate model of student life in which King’s designs around how students actually live, tests the wider King’s Edge proposition against that diversity, and creates richer opportunities to participate wherever students encounter the university.
problemSolved: King’s wider student experience is not yet consistently designed around the different ways students live, study and participate, making access to community, opportunity and belonging easier for some student forms than others.
whatChanges: King’s uses evidence-led student personas to design and assure a richer physical and digital student life, creating more vibrant campuses and meaningful routes into participation for students who are less or never campus-present.

caseForChange.problem:
The wider experience of university is an important part of what students should be able to expect from King’s. Relationships, communities, extracurricular opportunities, informal encounters and a sense of belonging all contribute to how students experience university and to the wider value they derive from it.

At present, access to that experience can depend too heavily on a traditional model of student life in which students spend substantial unstructured time on campus and discover opportunities simply by being there. That model fits some students well, but many students now combine study with long commutes, substantial paid work, caring responsibilities, placements, disability, financial pressure or patterns of digital and distance learning.

King’s also does not yet have a sufficiently systematic way of asking whether its wider student experience works across these different forms of student life. Individual initiatives may be inclusive in isolation while the combined experience remains significantly easier to access for some students than others.

At the same time, King’s has an expansive and distinctive estate with much greater potential to contribute actively to student life. Too often students can arrive for scheduled activity and leave again without encountering the communities, opportunities and experiences around them.
caseForChange.opportunity:
King’s can design student life more deliberately around the different ways its students actually live and study.

A small set of evidence-led student personas or participation archetypes can make this diversity tangible and usable. Applied across King’s Edge, they can help test whether opportunities are discoverable, participation is realistic, digital and physical routes are credible, and students with different patterns of time and presence can accumulate meaningful relationships, experiences and social capital.

King’s can combine this with a more ambitious approach to the physical student experience. Campuses can become richer, more vibrant and more festival-like, with frequent visible invitations to participate through pop-ups, performances, showcases, communities, skills activity, cultural experiences, employer and alumni encounters, student-led activity and other low-friction opportunities.

A meaningful digital twin can extend the same philosophy beyond the estate, creating authentic ways for students to encounter people, communities, events and opportunities without treating online participation as a lesser substitute for campus life.
caseForChange.whyNow:
The assumption that students will simply spend time on campus and discover university life incidentally is increasingly unrealistic. Commuting, paid work, caring responsibilities and financial pressure have changed patterns of student presence, while King’s has also expanded digital and distance education and intends to grow further.

At the same time, King’s is investing significantly in the opportunities available beyond the course. The value of that investment will depend on whether students with very different lives can actually find, enter and benefit from those opportunities.

There is therefore an opportunity to establish inclusion and participation as design requirements from the outset, while also making more ambitious use of King’s physical and digital environments as places where student life happens.
caseForChange.intendedChange:
King’s develops a clear picture of the different ways students live, study and participate, and uses this actively in the design and assurance of King’s Edge.

Students encounter richer and more frequent invitations to participate wherever they engage with the university. Campuses feel more alive, sociable and permeable, with activity and opportunity embedded into the everyday experience of being at King’s. Students who are less or never campus-present encounter an equally intentional digital environment through which they can participate in communities, experiences and opportunities.

Across King’s Edge, the student personas provide a continuing test of whether the programme works for the diversity of student lives it is intended to serve, exposing gaps and informing future investment, commissioning and design.
